prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual contributions to understanding how technological change, task content and trade shocks reshape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour markets

statement.case_for: B014 combines a clear conceptual framing (skill-biased change, the education-technology race, task-based labour demand) with research designs that are transparent and have been stress-tested for a long time. The skill-premium findings have been reproduced across countries and periods. The China-shock designs have drawn replication, re-analysis and critique over roughly a decade, and the qualitative conclusion about concentrated, persistent local adjustment costs has survived that scrutiny even though the magnitudes remain debated. That record of scrutiny is the main reason I weight this work above candidates whose empirical identification is more indirect. The topic also has a large policy audience and is relevant to current debates on AI and automation. Autor links both strands, Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, and Katz anchors the long-run skill-premium literature. That makes three names that map onto distinct, identifiable contributions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the discovery combines two strands (task-based technology and trade shocks) that a committee might see as two achievements, and the three-name cap cannot cover both cleanly. Dorn is a core co-author on the trade-shock papers and is excluded. Part of the theoretical task framework is attributable to people outside the credited names, notably Acemoglu and Restrepo. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still contested. Opening support for B014 is broad but shallow (one first place and three top-three rankings), so the committee may simply regard other candidates as stronger.

responses.point: Hassler proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn for B014, treating Katz as belonging to the earlier skill-biased technical change tradition. He sees overlap with Goldin's 2023 prize and Acemoglu's 2024 prize that reduces the unique contribution.
responses.response: The Dorn-versus-Katz choice is a real judgment call, and Dorn's role in the trade-shock papers is hard to dispute. I still keep Katz because the skill-premium and education-technology work is what makes this a labour-demand discovery rather than only a trade episode. It also has the longest record of replication. On overlap, I read the 2023 and 2024 citations as being about women's labour-market history and institutions and prosperity, so the overlap with task-based labour demand is thematic and not a duplication of the recognised achievement. I accept that this weakens the case somewhat, and I would be open to Dorn if the committee wants a purely trade-shock-centred citation.

responses.point: Krusell proposes only Autor and Hanson for B014. He notes that the theoretical task framework owes much to Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not credited, and that the robustness of some trade-shock estimates is still under discussion.
responses.response: I agree that the theoretical credit for the task framework is partly outside the credited names, and that is the main reason I word the citation around empirical and conceptual contributions rather than a task-model theory. I would not go to two names, though. Dropping Katz would leave the citation resting on the trade-shock evidence, whose persistence is the more debated strand, and would drop the older skill-premium findings that have the strongest replication record. I take the robustness concern seriously. It is why I regard the case as strong on qualitative findings and less settled on magnitudes.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B011 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He sees the 1997 paper as a clear two-author origin of the collateral-amplification mechanism and a clean theoretical contribution, and he would leave out Gertler and Gilchrist because of the overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I agree with Andersson on attribution. B011 has the cleanest credit line on the list, and it is why I rank it third and name it as an alternative. My hesitation is about evidence and not about originality. The collateral channel is identified indirectly, and the 2022 prize covered adjacent ground on financial crises. I would not call these disqualifying, and I accept that on attribution B011 is easier to defend than B014. I do not read the number of first-place votes as evidence about relative scientific merit, so my preference between the two rests on how well each result has been tested against data.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the task/technology and trade-shock strands as one achievement or two, and whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name.
How much of the task-framework credit sits with Acemoglu and Restrepo, who are not among the credited names.
The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects remain debated, and their long-run interpretation may change.

Whether the credit-boundary and 2022-overlap concerns about B011, or the Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum attribution gap in B005, are more serious than the maturity and attribution concerns about B014. My assessments rely on general knowledge and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and networks (Johannesson, Camerer, Brodeur, the Harvard evolutionary-dynamics group) are in metascience and experimental economics and do not overlap with the credited names in B014, B011 or B005.
